changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For buyers who already track checkout failures, lead with their own number instead of our average: 'You told us about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, worse on the big baskets. Here is what recovering those orders is worth to you in dollars, from your own decline data.' Keep the explanation of why big-ticket orders get knocked back as the lead proof point, and make the decline-value analysis (a three-month export of their declines) a standard step before pricing.
changes.why: We showed the average-uplift slide, but the decider still saw 'the same thing'. The champion responded to the decline explanation and already had her own failure figure, and our SE had offered to turn that figure into a dollar value.

changes.change: When we cannot reach the finance decider, give the champion a one-page CFO business case she can present without us. Put total cost (rate, gateway fee, chargeback handling) next to recovered revenue from failed orders, so the decision page never shrinks to a side-by-side of rates. Offer it as soon as a champion asks for something to 'hand' the CFO.
changes.why: The champion asked for 'a one-page business case' to hand the CFO and received a deck and a pricing proposal. The CFO then decided on a controller's page that showed only 'Our rate, their rate, side by side'.

changes.change: For incumbent bank processors that answer with a rate cut, add a counter-line we raise before the rate comparison: 'A better rate doesn't fix orders dying at the last step.' Pair it with the buyer's own failure rate and its dollar cost, so a matched or lower rate still reads as an unsolved problem.
changes.why: The bank's only move was 'Just a better rate', with 'No new product', while the customer still had no straight answer on why orders failed. After that, every email was about the rate, and even the rep concedes a matched rate would still have read as 'why move'.

changes.change: In ecommerce pain messaging, use the customer's language instead of 'acceptance' and 'uplift': 'orders dying at the last step', 'the big baskets', and the moment when 'we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no.' Attach a dollar figure to it.
changes.why: The champion described the problem as lost sales on expensive orders, while our acceptance-rate language let the CFO frame it as 'the same thing'.
